opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, this is one of the trickiest parts of the whole agenda. If you had reliable expert labels for everything, you wouldn't need scalable oversight in the first place. So you have to be a bit clever about constructing settings where you *do* know the ground truth, even though the overseer you're testing doesn't.

One approach I like is what people have called "sandwiching." You pick a task where the model is more capable than some group of non-expert humans, but less capable than actual domain experts. Then you give the non-experts whatever oversight technique you're studying, whether that's debate, critiques, decomposition, or AI assistance more generally, and you ask: does this let them get close to expert-level judgments? The experts are only used at the end to score how well it worked. They're not in the loop. That gives you a measurable signal today for a problem that's ultimately about the future.

A related trick is to create the gap artificially. You can take a weaker model as a stand-in for the human overseer and a stronger model as the thing being overseen, and see how much of the stronger model's capability you can elicit or verify. That's roughly the weak-to-strong generalization framing. It's not a perfect analogy, since models fail differently than people do, but it's cheap, you can run lots of experiments, and you know the right answers.

Another thing I think is underrated is deliberately planting flaws. You take outputs, introduce subtle bugs or errors that you know about, and measure whether your oversight setup catches them. With critique models, for example, you can ask: how often does the assisted human find the inserted bug compared to an unassisted human? Because you put the bug there, you have ground truth. You can even go adversarial and train a model to produce flaws that are as hard to spot as possible, which gives you a kind of red-team estimate of how robust the oversight really is.

And then there's a family of approaches that leans on consistency rather than correctness. If you can't check whether an answer is right, you can sometimes check whether the system is coherent: does it give the same answer under paraphrase, does it agree with itself when you break the problem into pieces, do its claims hold up when checked against things you *can* verify? That doesn't prove correctness, but inconsistency is a strong red flag.

The honest caveat is that all of these are proxies. The thing we actually care about is the regime where models are much smarter than us on tasks we can't check, and by construction we can't fully test that in advance. So I think the right posture is to build a portfolio of these evaluations, look for techniques that keep working as the capability gap widens, and pay a lot of attention to the trend lines. If a method's advantage holds up or grows as the gap gets bigger, that's real evidence. If it quietly degrades, that's exactly what we need to know before we're relying on it.

r001.rationale: The response describes planting known bugs to measure whether oversight catches them, but does not say this establishes which code version is worse.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, this is one of the central problems, and I think it's actually the thing that makes scalable oversight hard to study rather than just hard to build. If you had reliable expert labels, you wouldn't need scalable oversight in the first place. So you're always in this slightly awkward position where the thing you want to measure is precisely the thing you can't directly measure.

The approach I find most promising is what people sometimes call sandwiching. The idea is you take a task where you have three tiers: a non-expert human, the model, and a genuine expert. You pick a domain where the model is more capable than the non-expert but less capable than the expert. Then you ask: can the non-expert, using some oversight technique, reach a judgment that matches what the expert would have said? The expert labels exist, but they're held out. They're only used to score the experiment, not to run it. So you're simulating the future situation where humans are below the model, while still having ground truth to check against.

The obvious objection is that this only works as long as there's some expert who's above the model. At some point that stops being true, and then the sandwich collapses. So I think of sandwiching as a way to validate your methods now, in the regime where you can still check, and build up a track record that lets you trust those methods a bit further out.

Beyond that, there are a few other handles. One is consistency checks. Even if you can't verify an answer directly, you can check whether the model's answers hang together. If it tells you one thing when asked directly and something contradictory when you decompose the problem, that's a signal, and you didn't need an expert to find it. Debate and similar setups lean on this a lot. The protocol is designed so that a dishonest answer is hard to defend against a competent opponent, and the human only needs to judge the local arguments, not the whole thing.

Another handle is synthetic tasks where you plant the ground truth. You deliberately construct problems with known answers, or you insert known flaws into code or proofs, and you see whether the oversight process catches them. The weakness is that planted flaws might not look like naturally occurring ones, so you have to be careful about generalization. But it gives you a clean signal.

And then there's the honest answer, which is that some of this will come down to adversarial evaluation of the models themselves. You take a model, you deliberately train it to be subtly wrong or to game the overseer, and you test whether your oversight stack notices. That's uncomfortable, but it's one of the few ways to get a lower bound on how robust the method is.

The thing I'd push back on is the framing that we need to solve the whole problem before we can make progress. We don't need a metric that works in the limit. We need enough evidence from the regimes we can check that we're justified in extending a bit of trust into the regimes we can't. And we need to be very explicit about where that trust runs out.

r001.rationale: The response mentions inserting known flaws into code to test whether oversight catches them, but does not say this establishes which code version is worse.

astra-6.text:
I think the central difficulty is that, ultimately, you want to evaluate oversight in precisely the cases where you can’t easily tell whether the model’s answer is correct. So there isn’t a single clean benchmark that resolves this.

One approach is to create a gap in capability or information in a setting where we can still check the outcome. You give the overseer less information, or less time, than would ordinarily be needed to solve the task, and then ask whether assistance from a stronger model lets them make good judgments. You can compare those judgments with an answer that you’ve held back from the overseer. That gives you evidence about whether the oversight process actually helps, although it doesn’t establish that the same thing will work at much higher capability levels.

You can also deliberately introduce mistakes and test whether the overseer catches them, including mistakes chosen to be persuasive or difficult to detect. And where possible, you want tasks with outcomes you can eventually verify, even if you can’t judge the answer immediately.

But I’d distinguish those tests from validating oversight when nobody has reliable ground truth. In that setting, agreement between models or a convincing explanation isn’t enough: they could share the same mistake. So I’d want several different sources of evidence, and I’d still expect substantial uncertainty. The important question is how far those experiments justify trusting the oversight process beyond the settings where we can directly check it.

r001.rationale: The response mentions deliberately introducing mistakes to test whether an overseer catches them, but it does not identify bug insertion in code or compare code versions to determine which is worse.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the central difficulty is that if we could reliably judge the answer ourselves, we wouldn’t really be testing the thing we ultimately need scalable oversight for. We want to know whether an oversight process helps us distinguish good work from work that merely looks convincing, even when the system knows more than we do.

One way to make progress is to create that gap deliberately. You can give the model access to information that the human evaluator doesn’t have, or ask a nonexpert to oversee a task where an expert can check the result afterward. Then you can compare unaided judgment with judgment assisted by the oversight method. Does the assistance actually help people identify mistakes? And does that still work when another model is actively trying to get a bad answer accepted?

But those are proxies. If reliable expert labels are unavailable altogether, you need to look for other sources of evidence: predictions you can eventually check, consequences you can test, or independently verifiable pieces of a larger argument. Agreement between several models isn’t enough by itself, because they could share the same blind spots.

So I’d want a collection of evaluations that test different failure modes, especially under adversarial pressure. That can build confidence, but there’s still an important gap between showing that oversight works in settings we can check and knowing that it works beyond our ability to check.

r001.rationale: The response discusses creating evaluation gaps and testing whether oversight detects mistakes, but it does not identify deliberate bug insertion or compare code versions to establish which is worse.
